chunks: Challenges when testing PCBs. The question: What are some challenges when testing PCBs?
Testing a board is hard for several reasons. You often cannot reach the point you want to measure, because of hidden chip pins. Your probe changes the circuit it measures.
Faults can hide, for example a crack that opens only when the board is warm.
And when something fails, it is unclear whether the cause is the design, the assembly, the firmware, or your test setup.
Imagine taking the temperature of a thimble of tea with a huge thermometer.
The thermometer soaks up heat and cools the tea, so you read a number that is not the original temperature. A probe does the same to a circuit.
It adds a bit of capacitance and resistance, and on a delicate node that changes the answer.
Both probes look like their full resistance only below a couple of kilohertz; above that the capacitance takes over and the impedance falls as 1/f.
At 100 megahertz the 10x probe is about 130 ohms and the 1x about 16 ohms, so probing a high-impedance node can change what you measure.
Test point: a small exposed pad on a connection, put there so you can probe it. Probe loading: the extra capacitance and resistance a probe adds to the node it touches.
Spring ground: a very short ground connection for a probe. A long clip lead rings and invents noise.
Intermittent fault: a problem that comes and goes, such as a cracked joint that opens when warm.
Boundary scan: a way to check connections between chips, even under chips whose pins are hidden beneath them, through special pins.
A typical oscilloscope probe adds about 12 picofarads of capacitance, a tiny charge store. Touch it to a node fed through a 100 kilohms resistor.
The two form a low-pass filter, which passes slow signals and weakens fast ones above a corner frequency of 1 over (2 pi times 100 kilohms times 12 picofarads ) , about 133 kilohertz.
At 1 megahertz the scope would show only about 13% of the true signal. The circuit may be fine, and the probe is the problem.
That is the whole idea: measuring changes the circuit, and access limits what you can measure.

"The main challenges are access, since BGAs, inner layers and tiny pads hide nodes; measurement effects, because probes load the circuit and long ground leads ring; localising shorts and intermittent faults; telling hardware, assembly, firmware and setup problems apart; and doing all this at scale with fixtures and coverage.
I plan test points, use proper probing, and isolate variables one at a time."
